en: The similarities are unmistakable—likely based on the aforementioned work.

Judging by the numeration, this must have once formed part of a composite codex, most probably one similar to the *Rakṣācakravidhayaḥ* or *Varṣāpanavidhayaḥ*, wherein similar paraphrases are found. I have no doubt that this is based on the work of Vaidyapāda, of which, to my knowledge, nothing survives in Sanskrit.
Input: Péter-Dániel Szántó [42r] Homage to the Buddha!
The yellow Vajrin, with a thousand eyes, is mounted upon a white Airāvata;
to his left is the black Viṣṇu, whose vehicle is Garuḍa. (1)
Holding a mace and a discus in his right hand, and bearing a conch and the Kaustubha gem in his left,
the thick-bodied one, filled with flames, is considered Pāvaka in the southeast. (2)
Red in color, with a crown of tawny matted hair, seated upon a goat, and holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and an eye;
he is joined by [deities] similar to himself, and in his left [hands] he holds a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). (3)
In the southern [direction] is blue Yama, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, seated upon a buffalo;
his tawny hair blazes upward, and his hands hold a staff and make the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
(4) What follows that?
In the southwest is Asita Kravyāda, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a corpse;
he is naked, his face terrifying with fangs, deformed, and has hair standing erect. (5)
Bearing a skull-bowl, the terrifying Varuṇa is held to be in the western direction;
he holds a serpent-noose, is white in color, possesses a large body, and has a swan as his vehicle. (6) In the north-western direction is Vāyu, green in color, seated upon a yellow deer.
In the north, between Vātapaṭāpada and Ūrmi, is Cakraveraka.
(7) [He is] yellow, seated on a man, corpulent, and holding a *nakulī* and a *bījapūra*.
White, seated upon a mouse, is Mahodhara, the commander-in-chief of Māra’s army. (8)
To his left is one resembling a lordly elephant, holding a radish, an axe, and a staff;
in the northeast is the auspicious Īśvara, mounted upon a bull, bearing matted hair and bones, with a *khaṭvāṅga* and a *ḍamaru* drum held busily in his hands, and a great radiance rising upward. (9)
Mounted upon Ambariṣa, he is red in color and has a red lotus as his banner. To his left is Candra, seated upon a white water-lily and holding white dice.
Above those two is Brahmā, yellow in color, holding a staff and dice, and seated upon a swan.
Vemacitri has thick limbs, wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), has matted hair, is short in stature, and possesses four faces.
He is dark below, holds a sword, and stands upon the sun.
To his left is the Earth, yellow in color, seated upon a lotus, and holding a water-pot (*kumbha*).
With their left hands in a graceful pose and their right hands grasping their respective banners, all are depicted without crowns, possessing two arms and jeweled head-ornaments.
These World Protectors of great supernatural power reside in their own established directions within the world-systems. (13–14)

Adorned with divine ornaments radiant with the luster of various jewels, they have dispelled all darkness by the splendor of their bodies resulting from [past] maturation. Together with their respective complete armies, kinsmen, wives, and so forth, [they approach]. (15)
"Drawn in by the hook [produced] from the array of light radiating from the seed-syllable in the heart by means of the wrathful wheel.
(16) Thus is the summary indication. || 0 ||
With ten wrathful deities born from the heart-rays, their lower bodies as pillars and their upper arms raised, possessing six arms,
holding a kila and a vajra-hammer in their hands,
with wrath flashing from the fire of their hearts, and appearing in the forms of one’s own chosen deities. (17)
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Yamāntakṛt, nail-pierce all the wicked ones, including Indra and Upendra, together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! O Prajñāntakṛt, nail down all the wicked Yamas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Padmāntakṛt, nail down all malevolent nāgas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! O Vighnāntakṛt, nail down all the wicked Kuveras and Gaṇapatis, together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Ṭakki, nail down all malevolent fires together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Nīladaṇḍa, nail down all malevolent nairṛtas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! O Mahābala, nail down all wicked winds together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Acala, nail down all the malevolent Īśānas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ bhrūṃ! O Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, nail down all evil ones—the sun, the moon, and the Grandfather (Brahmā)—along with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Sumbha! All evil Vemacitrin and earth deities, together with your retinues, be impaled! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Thus, by those reciting [the mantra], they were each individually pinned down by the practitioners of the yoga of the knowledge of equality regarding the pins and so forth, who destroy the obscurations,
and who embrace the limbs of their own captivating wisdom-consorts as members of the assembly. (18)

Pervading the sky of their respective directions, accompanied by their own retinues and so forth, they arise with three faces and six arms, radiant with various ornaments. Upon the moon is Vajrāyudha, yellow in color, holding a vajra, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus. (19–20)
Nīla is blue, marked with the signs of a wheel, sword, and conch, and stands upon the *māyā* seed-syllable on the sun disk;
he has three eyes, wears a crown of matted hair, is red in color, and holds the gestures of fearlessness and the eye.
(21) Vajrakāla is fat, black, and stands upon the sun disk; he holds a water-pot and a staff.
Marked by a staff, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus, with tawny beard and hair,
standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, holding a thunderbolt, a mace, a sword, a skull-bowl, and a jewel in his hands, and possessing the luster of a lotus, he stands within a solar disc.
The five [deities] beginning with Vajrāyudha should be known as having Akṣobhya upon their crowns.
(23) Here, Citri, Sauṇḍa, Prabha, and Krūra are the four who possess Sāvitra.
Nāga, Vajra, Sita, and Srita hold a nāga, a vajra, a sword, and a jewel-lotus respectively. (24)

Vākkula, residing in the moon, is of the Vajra family; Amoghasiddhi, the lord of the Indu family, has hands marked with a garment, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus, and resembles a Palāśa flower. Bhairava and Hemābha hold a citron and a sword.
On the right he holds a lotus upon which the sun rests, and on the left he bears a mongoose;
(26) Vajraśauṇḍaka holds lotuses and Modāpinī;
he is white, seated upon the moon, known as Vajrakrodha, and adorned with bones. (27)
He is remembered as having lotus-hands holding a trident, a sword, a jewel, and a lotus;
Vajrakuṇḍalin is red, bearing a lotus, a sword, a discus, and a ruby.
Ratnakula is in the sun; Vajraprabha is white, resting upon the moon.
[He is] yellow, holding a white lotus, a sword, and a lotus, with the moon as his crest. Maunavajra is considered to hold a lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a discus;
he has a discus on his crown. At the sun [is] Vemacitrin, the blue lord of the asuras. (29–30)
Cakradhara holds a wheel in his right hand and a jewel-lotus in his left; the yellow goddess Pṛthivī resides within the Lord of the Kāyavajra family.
She bears a lotus, a sword, a wheel, and a jewel, and is united with her own consort.
Seated upon petals on their own lotuses, they rest within their respective circles of light.
Māyā, Nalī, Yamā, Kṛtyā, Yakṣī, Kuṇḍalī, and Citri are mounted upon radiant mandalas; the remaining ones are within circles of smoke.
The Protectors are seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture; they are profound and have the form of Hari.
All wear crowns of rubies and are radiant with the primary and secondary marks of perfection.
Jaṃ hūṃ ruṃ kaṃ suṃ vaṃ paṃ nāṃ soṃ māḥ | āṃ veṃ aṃ oṃ laṃ ||
And their causes, which carry away [all] darkness, reside within the moon in the heart;
they dwell within the circle of the melting Vajradhara situated inside the lotus of innate gnosis. (35) Through the intention...
[of] the latent tendencies and afflictions—
preceded by non-violence, the mantra is entered with the intellect.
Oṃ āḥ Heruka vajrasamaya hrīḥ! O destroyer of the mudrās of all wicked samayas, remove the faults of their intentions! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Homage to the Vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all; homage to the Vajra Wrathful One, the Great Fanged and Terrifying One, who holds a sword, a mace, a spear, and a noose in his hands. Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali! Kha kha khāhi khāhi! Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha! Bandha bandha! Hana hana! Daha daha! Garja garja! Visphoṭaya visphoṭaya! Drive away all obstacles and impediments, even Mahāgaṇapati! Destroy the latent defilements and faults of these [obstructors]! Hūṃ Phaṭ!
Having prepared [the offering] equal in number to the sky of all worlds with substances according to the ritual procedure,
through the conviction that Vajrasattva has arisen from the sequence of the five aspects.
Through the entry of each individual *bodhicitta* into the state of fluidity,
the groups originating from Locanā and the others are condensed into twenty-one clusters.
Manifested from the signs of their own seed-syllables, they take the forms of Kṣitigarbha and the other bodhisattvas;
pervading all space are the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements.
Their characteristics are well-known; they have two arms embracing their respective consorts.
For all of them, the right face is black, while for the one who is black, the face is white.

Likewise, for these [afflictions], the left [pulse] is white; however, in cases of pustules and the like, or when there is a great flow [of blood], it is red in those with white or black complexions, [diagnosed] by means of the *māsaka* measures ending with fish and meat.
Having seen before him [the vessel] filled with milk, lamps, water, as well as foods to be licked and sucked, and provided with offerings, perfumes, and so forth;
With song, dance, and instrumental music, with parasols, banners, and canopies,
and with divine articles of worship, the offering was thus arrayed.
In the absence [of a vessel], one should use a shallow bowl or similar container for food, water, and drinks;
or whatever else is obtained, at the proper time and according to the prescribed rule.
The yogi, having duly prepared his own golden maṇḍala,
[should worship] the ten seed-syllables within the lotus with beautiful flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped them with hands joined together, impelled by the rays from his own heart,
and intent on embracing her with his left arm, [he should worship her] consecrated by the garland-mantra.

Having placed the *hūṃ* and the vajra upon the tongue, and with a mind characterized by the equality of all things such as food and drink, one should thereby satisfy all those [beings] as well as oneself, the holder of the wheel (*cakrin*).
Having worshipped them as before, and having praised them while they were satisfied with the flowing sounds of the bell,
he should inform them of his desired aim— those [deities] who are preceded by the granting of accomplishments.
Having observed the clamorous sounds emitted there by those who were speaking with one voice, "That is excellent! Release it! one should ask for forgiveness and dismiss them. ||o||
This is the mantra for the empowerment of the offering (bali).

Oṃ Āḥ! All the world-protectors and all sentient beings throughout the three times and the ten directions, who abide in the presence within the continuous succession of mandalas of atoms pervading the vast array of ocean-like space in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions of the three times; who have converged in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); who extend to the limits of the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*); and who are equal to the sky in their pervasive array of infinite clouds throughout the world-systems of the three times and ten directions.

Namely: Vajrāyudha, Māyāvajra, Vajrānala, Kālavajra, Muṣalanāga, Nāgavajra, Vajrānala, Vajrabhairava, Vajrasauṇḍa, Vajrakrodha, Vajrakuṇḍali, Vajraprabha, Maunavajra, Vemacitrin, and the Earth Deity, together with their retinues.

Accept this offering of bali, accompanied by flowers, incense, perfumes, scents, food offerings, and the like. Having partaken of it, for the sake of my gold, silver, wealth, grain, long life, youth, health, and true happiness, subdue, paralyze, and destroy all obstacles, impediments, and all wicked and malicious beings—whether human or non-human. [Grant] my gold, silver, wealth, grain, long life, youth, health, and true happiness for the increase of great bliss, until the very end at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Offer your assistance to me; grant peace and protection! HŪṂ DHRAṂ ĀḤ! O Muñjavajra, you who shatter all evil samaya-seals, grant me peace and protection, SVĀHĀ HŪṂ!
Oṃ! Having granted you the accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings, go as you please to the realm of the Buddhas, for the sake of returning again, *mur*.
Alternatively:
Oṃ Āḥ! The syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen; Hūṃ Muḥ! Thus it is said.
Or with a three-syllable mantra ending in the letter *mukāra*.
